chapters.title: Ch 2 · Software architecture, requirements and the 4+1 views
Ch 3 · Quality attributes, scenarios and tactics
Ch 5 · Principles of detailed design and SOLID
Ch 7 · Structural and behavioral design patterns

sources.title: Introduction to Software Design and Architecture

questions.q: IEEE defines software engineering as an approach that is systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable. What does “quantifiable” add to that definition?
o: Developer output is tracked by counting lines of code
Every phase must follow a fixed waterfall lifecycle
Costs are fixed in advance through fixed-price contracts with the client
Results are measured against stated targets, not judged by taste
questions.e: Quantifiable means outcomes are checked against measurable targets. Systematic means the work is repeatable and reviewable.

questions.q: A payment system stores money as a floating-point number. Why is it far cheaper to catch this in design review than after launch?
o: Column types cannot be changed at all once a database is running in production
Floating-point rounding only shows up during design review
Late, it becomes a data migration and repair instead of a type choice
Payment regulators audit designs but never running systems
questions.e: Cost of change grows roughly an order of magnitude per phase; the same defect costs a type choice early and a data-repair project late.

questions.q: A team frames a problem as: current portal deploys in 40 minutes; target is under 5; same Oracle database, no new servers. Which problem-solving element is “no new servers this year”?
questions.e: Constraints limit which candidate solutions are acceptable; the 40-minute deploy is the initial state and the 5-minute deploy is the goal state.

questions.q: Which decision is architectural rather than detailed design?
o: Using a HashMap keyed by SKU for the cart's line items
Splitting the system into catalog, cart, and payment services
Renaming a private helper method inside the payment module
Adding a Strategy class for each discount rule in the cart
questions.e: The service split fixes deployment boundaries, failure modes, and team ownership for years. The others are local and cheaply reversed.

questions.q: Which quick test best separates an architectural decision from a detailed-design one?
o: Whether a senior engineer or the team lead made it
Whether it is costly to reverse and affects many teams
Whether it appears on a UML class or package diagram
Whether it touches the database or the network layer
questions.e: Architectural decisions are high-impact and costly to undo; detailed-design decisions are local and cheap to replace.

questions.q: In architecture, which of these is an “externally visible property” of an element?
o: The names of its private fields
The performance other elements can rely on
The data structures inside its methods
The sorting algorithm it uses internally
questions.e: Externally visible properties are what other elements can depend on: provided services, performance, resource use. Internal implementation is hidden.

questions.q: What do architecture and detailed design have in common?
o: Both are expressed using only UML class diagrams
Both are completed before requirements are gathered
Both are owned, reviewed, and approved by the operations team before release
Both use abstraction and decomposition to manage complexity
questions.e: The two work at different scales but use the same complexity-management principles.

questions.q: Which stakeholder is most likely to put deployability and observability first?
questions.e: Users emphasize usability and reliability, developers modifiability, and operators deployability and observability.

questions.q: The operations team is shown a diagram of two web nodes behind a load balancer with a replicated database. That diagram is a…
questions.e: A viewpoint is the set of conventions and concerns ("show nodes and networks for operations"); the view is the actual representation that results.

questions.q: In a hospital system, the physician wants one-click chart access while compliance wants re-authentication every five minutes. What is the architect's job here?
o: Side with the most senior stakeholder and document the decision in the requirements
Remove both requirements until the stakeholders agree
Leave the conflict for developers to settle while coding
Make the trade-off explicit, e.g. short tokens plus a logged emergency path
questions.e: Conflicting concerns are normal; trade-offs must be explicit and justified, not left to chance.

questions.q: Why is identifying stakeholders treated as an architectural activity rather than a formality?
o: It lets the team skip writing quality attribute scenarios
Missed concerns return late as requirements the structure can't meet
Stakeholders must approve each module before it is coded
Every diagram must list its stakeholders to be considered valid
questions.e: Missing a stakeholder means missing their concerns, and those return late when changing the structure is costly.

questions.q: “Checkout must complete in under 2 seconds at 10,000 concurrent users.” Why is this an architectural driver while “the user can apply a coupon” usually is not?
o: Functional requirements are never architectural drivers
It concerns the user interface, which is always architectural
It was the first requirement written in the document
It forces structure: caching, replicas, async processing
questions.e: Drivers are the few requirements with major architectural influence. Most functional requirements do not change the structure.

questions.q: A university mandates its existing Oracle database and national data-residency rules. In driver terms these are…
questions.e: Constraints restrict choice before design starts, for example mandated technology, regulation, budget, or legacy integration.

questions.q: According to the chapter, when is a driver worth recording?
o: Whenever it is listed in the project charter
When you can name the structure it forces or rules out
When several stakeholders mention it in interviews
When it is a functional rather than a quality requirement
questions.e: A driver that changes nothing about the structure is not architecturally significant.

questions.q: Which requirement is most likely to be architecturally significant?
o: The help page must list support office hours and email
Customer data must stay behind a separate security boundary
Users can sort the course table by date, name, or instructor
The monthly report must show the title in bold at the top
questions.e: Architecturally significant functional requirements usually involve scale, distribution, security boundaries, or integration.

questions.q: In Attribute-Driven Design, what happens right after choosing the element to decompose?
o: Write the user manual for it
Pick the driving requirement for it
questions.e: ADD iterates: choose an element, pick its driver, select tactics and patterns, allocate responsibilities and interfaces, then verify.

questions.q: Tax rules change every fiscal year while the invoice layout is stable. What design move does the chapter recommend?
o: Put tax calculation in its own module with a versioned rule table
Merge tax and layout into one class so the two always change together in one release
Duplicate the tax logic in each invoice template
Hard-code the current year's rates for speed
questions.e: Decompose around change boundaries so the volatile part changes in one place.

questions.q: Before committing to a message broker, a team runs a two-day spike pushing 50,000 events through it. This is an example of…
o: Premature optimization of the messaging layer
questions.e: Scenarios, prototypes, reviews, and risk analysis validate a design early; measured evidence beats vendor claims.

questions.q: Why is design described as iterative rather than a single top-down pass?
o: Iteration is required by the IEEE definition
Each iteration must use a new technology
Analysis and prototypes reveal new drivers
questions.e: A single pass rarely survives the first prototype, because new knowledge changes the drivers.

questions.q: A six-person admin tool is given a plugin framework, a rules engine, and a message bus that are never used. This is mainly…
questions.e: Essential complexity comes from the problem; accidental complexity comes from our chosen solution and can be designed away.

questions.q: Which statement about “simplicity” matches the chapter?
o: Shipping the product with fewer features overall so there is less code to maintain
Avoiding design patterns and abstractions entirely
Using as few classes and files as possible
Fewer things to hold in mind to change one behavior safely
questions.e: Simplicity is about the mental load of safe change, not about feature count.

questions.q: A layered monolith suits a 3-person startup but not a 200-engineer platform needing independent deploys. What principle does this show?
o: Architecture matters only once a company is large
Monoliths are always the wrong choice for any team
Microservices are always the better choice for small teams that need to ship quickly
No architecture is universally best; fit depends on context
questions.e: Design quality is judged against stakeholder scenarios and context, not by a universal ranking.

questions.q: How should design quality be demonstrated?
o: By the age of the chosen technologies
By the number of diagrams produced
By aesthetic preference of the architect
questions.e: Good design is shown by meeting stakeholder scenarios, not by looks alone.

questions.q: Encrypting every field in a medical database breaks indexed search and adds latency. What does this illustrate?
o: Security measures never affect performance if they are designed well
Quality goals often conflict and need trade-offs
Sensitive fields should never be encrypted
Search speed is not a quality attribute
questions.e: Confidentiality and performance pull in opposite directions; the team chooses what to encrypt and records the remaining risk.

questions.q: Three teams each own one layer of a monolith, so every feature needs three coordinated releases. Which idea explains this?
questions.e: System structure mirrors team structure, so organizational boundaries should be designed alongside technical ones.

questions.q: An architect lacks the data to choose between two databases. Which response does the chapter treat as legitimate?
o: Picking whichever vendor is cheapest today
Choosing both and deciding in production
Deferring the decision until evidence exists
questions.e: Architects work with incomplete information; deliberately deferring a decision until evidence arrives is a valid design move.

questions.q: How does the chapter treat ethical and professional practices in design?
o: As design constraints, not optional extras
As optional work that can be skipped when the deadline is tight
As relevant only to AI systems
As a concern only for legal teams
questions.e: Professional obligations constrain design just like budget or regulation.

questions.q: Explain why fixing a defect costs more the later it is found. Give one example.
questions.m: Cost of change grows roughly an order of magnitude per phase. A money-as-float bug is a one-line type decision in design review but a schema migration, data repair, and bank reconciliation after launch.

questions.q: Distinguish an architectural decision from a detailed-design decision and give one example of each.
questions.m: Architectural decisions are expensive to reverse and affect many teams or qualities (splitting into catalog, cart, and payment services). Detailed-design decisions are local and cheap to change (a HashMap for cart items).

questions.q: What is the difference between a viewpoint and a view?
questions.m: A viewpoint defines the conventions, stakeholders, and concerns to address; a view is the actual representation produced by following it, such as the deployment diagram of a specific system.

questions.q: What makes a requirement an architectural driver? Give an example.
questions.m: A driver is one of the few requirements with major architectural influence: you can name the structure it forces. "Checkout under 2 s at 10,000 concurrent users" forces caching and replicas.

questions.q: Distinguish essential from accidental complexity.
questions.m: Essential complexity comes from the problem itself; accidental complexity comes from the solution we chose, such as unused frameworks, and can be designed away.

questions.q: Explain Conway's law and what it means for architects.
questions.m: System structure mirrors the communication structure of the teams that build it, so organizational boundaries should be designed together with technical boundaries.

questions.q: Why can't an architecture be captured in one diagram?
o: Standards forbid showing classes and servers together
Only the deployment diagram counts as architecture
Diagram tools limit how many boxes fit on a page
Module, runtime, and allocation structures can't be merged
questions.e: One module can map to many runtime components and vice versa, so multiple complementary structures are needed.

questions.q: Which question does a component-and-connector (C&C) view answer?
o: What is running and how does it communicate?
Where does it live and who owns it?
What can a developer change and what breaks?
questions.e: Module views cover change and dependencies; C&C views cover runtime interaction; allocation views cover placement and ownership.

questions.q: A PaymentValidator is deployed to two availability zones and owned by the Payments team. Which structure records this?
questions.e: Allocation structures map software to hardware, teams, files, or environments.

questions.q: The reporting module uses the ledger module but not the reverse. What does this one-way dependency allow?
o: Both modules must now always be built and deployed together as one unit
Reporting can be replaced without touching the ledger
The ledger can call reporting synchronously
The ledger can no longer be unit tested
questions.e: A uses structure shows dependency direction; a one-way dependency makes the dependent side replaceable.

questions.q: What does a viewpoint define?
o: The finished diagram produced for one specific system and its stakeholders
The list of alternatives the team rejected
The conventions, concerns, and rules for a kind of view
The schedule for deploying each component
questions.e: The viewpoint is the template; a view is what you produce with it.

questions.q: A regulator asks where personal data crosses a network boundary. Which view answers this?
o: A deployment view with trust zones
A class diagram of the domain
A sequence diagram of the login flow
questions.e: Choose views by the stakeholder question they answer; only a deployment view with trust zones shows network boundaries.

questions.q: The process view shows an async event from Order to Shipping, but the module view shows Shipping calling Order directly. What is this?
o: Proof that the process view is optional
A harmless difference in drawing style
Normal, because each view is an independent model and may disagree with others
A real defect: the views contradict each other
questions.e: Views describe one system, so a contradiction between them means something is wrong.

questions.q: According to the chapter, a view without a key and defined element semantics is…
o: Preferable, because simpler diagrams read faster
Decoration: boxes and lines with no agreed meaning
Acceptable as long as the audience is technical
Required for the scenario view in 4+1
questions.e: Without a key, readers invent their own meaning for each symbol.

questions.q: Which activity belongs to requirements elicitation?
o: Prioritizing, classifying, and negotiating the collected requirements
Observing users and running facilitated meetings
questions.e: Elicitation gathers requirements (interviews, meetings, observation, scenarios); analysis classifies, prioritizes, and negotiates them.

questions.q: “The system shall be fast.” What is the main problem?
o: It is a design constraint rather than a requirement, so it belongs elsewhere
It is not verifiable, so it cannot be tested
questions.e: A verifiable version is "95% of searches return within 300 ms with 500 concurrent users".

questions.q: A data-protection law requires erasure on request; the team infers it needs a single deletion API. The law and the inferred API are, respectively…
questions.e: Imposed requirements come from outside (law, standards, policy); derived ones are consequences the team infers.

questions.q: What does traceability connect?
questions.e: Example chain: expand to the EU → support GDPR erasure → isolate user data behind a deletion API → integration test proves deletion.

questions.q: Which property is NOT on the chapter's list of good requirement qualities?
o: Written in the team's technical jargon
Verifiable by a test or measurement
questions.e: Good requirements are specific, consistent, correct, attainable, complete, and verifiable.

questions.q: How do quality attribute scenarios help nonfunctional requirements?
o: They are only written after deployment
They make them testable with a measure
They remove the need for stakeholders
questions.e: A scenario gives a stimulus, context, and response measure that can pass or fail.

questions.q: In Kruchten's 4+1 model, which view primarily serves programmers and uses component or package diagrams?
questions.e: Logical serves end users, process serves integrators, development serves programmers, and physical serves system engineers.

questions.q: Why are scenarios the “+1” in 4+1?
o: They replace the physical view for cloud systems
They are optional and only used in large systems
They describe how the system is built and packaged
They validate the other four by tracing use cases
questions.e: A use case such as "student registers" must be traceable through the logical, process, development, and physical views.

questions.q: Which diagram types typically represent the logical view?
questions.e: The logical view shows functionality in terms of classes and their interactions.

questions.q: A deployment diagram reveals that a reporting job and live registration share one database node. Which 4+1 view exposed this?
questions.e: The physical view maps software onto hardware nodes and exposes shared-resource problems.

questions.q: For “student registers for a course,” the seat-reservation transaction and its locking appear in which view?
questions.e: The process view covers concurrency, transactions, and runtime behavior.

questions.q: Which set of fields belongs in an Architecture Decision Record (ADR)?
o: Class names, method signatures, and test coverage
Context, decision, alternatives, consequences, and status
Author, reviewers, team size, deadline, budget, and approval signatures
Server addresses, ports, and deployment credentials
questions.e: An ADR preserves why a decision was made, what was rejected, and what it costs.

questions.q: Why record rejected alternatives in an ADR?
o: Because auditors require a minimum number of options
To record who proposed each of the bad options
So settled debates don't reopen when context is forgotten
So the alternatives can be built later in parallel
questions.e: Recorded rejections preserve the reasoning that settled a question.

questions.q: A team hard-codes a currency table to hit a launch date, records it with a review date, and replaces it next quarter. This is…
questions.e: Technical debt is a future obligation; here it was taken knowingly and tracked.

questions.q: Which sequence shows a valid ADR status lifecycle?
o: Open → in review → closed → reopened whenever someone disagrees
questions.e: Status keeps the record honest as the system evolves.

questions.q: Two services exchange {"amount": 1050}; one means halalas, the other riyals. The schema validates. What kind of mismatch is this?
questions.e: Syntax agreed but meaning differed. Contracts must cover semantics, not just format.

questions.q: What does documenting only an element's provided interface hide?
o: The names of its internal classes
Its full version and release history
How it performs under peak load
What the element requires from others
questions.e: An interface has provided and required sides; both are dependencies.

questions.q: A payments API adds an optional field and postpones removing a deprecated one until a v2 endpoint. Which contract aspect is being managed?
questions.e: Additive changes keep old clients working; breaking changes wait for a new version.

questions.q: What makes the semantic half of a contract checkable rather than conversational?
o: A switch from XML payloads to JSON with a published schema file
questions.e: Formal conditions state exactly what must hold before and after a call.

questions.q: Code violates the intended layering, while separately the documentation still shows one deployable after the team split off two services. These are, respectively…
questions.e: Erosion is code violating the intended structure; drift is the design evolving without the documentation following.

questions.q: An ArchUnit test fails the build if any domain class imports infrastructure. What is this called?
o: A quality attribute scenario with a response measure
questions.e: Fitness functions turn architectural rules into automated checks that CI can enforce.

questions.q: Which statement about architecture governance matches the chapter?
o: Nothing once the architecture document is signed
Manual approval of every commit by the architect
questions.e: Architecture is not a one-time artifact; governance keeps it consistent over time with minimal overhead.

questions.q: Name the three kinds of architectural structure and the question each answers.
questions.m: Module structures: what can a developer change and what breaks. Component-and-connector: what runs and how it talks. Allocation: where it lives and who owns it.

questions.q: List the 4+1 views and explain why scenarios are the +1.
questions.m: Logical, process, development, and physical views, plus scenarios that validate them by tracing use cases through all four.

questions.q: Rewrite "the system shall be fast" as a verifiable requirement and explain why it is better.
questions.m: "95% of catalog searches return within 300 ms with 500 concurrent users." It can be measured and can fail, so it is verifiable.

questions.q: What goes into an ADR and why record rejected alternatives?
questions.m: Context, decision, alternatives, consequences, and status. Recording rejected alternatives stops the same debate reopening when context is forgotten.

questions.q: Give an example of a semantic interface mismatch.
questions.m: Two services agree on {"amount": 1050}, but one means halalas and the other riyals. The syntax validates while the meaning is wrong.

questions.q: Distinguish architectural erosion from architectural drift.
questions.m: Erosion is code violating the intended structure; drift is the design evolving without the documentation following.

questions.q: Which list gives the six parts of a quality attribute scenario?
o: Actor, use case, precondition, postcondition, trigger, priority
Risk, threat, asset, control, owner, date
Source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response, response measure
Input, process, output, storage, feedback, control
questions.e: The six parts turn a quality wish into an analyzable requirement.

questions.q: In an availability scenario, “normal operation at peak hours” is the…
questions.e: The environment is the system state when the stimulus arrives; acceptable responses differ between normal and degraded conditions.

questions.q: “Service restored within 30 seconds with no committed order lost” is the scenario's…
questions.e: The response is what the system does (promote the standby); the measure is how it is judged.

questions.q: What is the difference between general and concrete scenarios?
o: General ones are reusable templates; concrete ones are system-specific
General ones have measures; concrete ones leave the measure out
General ones cover security only; concrete ones cover all qualities
Concrete ones omit the environment; general ones always include it
questions.e: A general scenario is instantiated with system-specific values to make a concrete one.

questions.q: Why does the scenario's environment matter?
o: It names the programming language and framework
Acceptable responses differ under normal load and overload
It replaces the need for a response measure by describing load conditions
It records which analyst wrote the scenario
questions.e: The same stimulus can have different acceptable outcomes depending on system state.

questions.q: A discount rate moves from a compile-time constant to a config file to a runtime rules table. Which design decision category is this?
questions.e: Later binding buys flexibility (marketing can change it without a deploy) and adds failure modes.

questions.q: A thread pool capped at 200 with a bounded queue protects a service during a spike. This is a decision about…
questions.e: Bounded resources degrade gracefully; an unbounded pool briefly serves more, then dies from memory exhaustion.

questions.q: Which decision category decides what can scale, fail, or be released independently?
o: The UI color scheme and layout grid
Naming conventions for variables and classes
The format of the project's data dictionary
Mapping elements to runtime and deployment units
questions.e: How elements map to processes and nodes sets the units of scaling, failure, and release.

questions.q: Why report p95 and p99 latency instead of the average?
o: Averages hide the users who suffer during spikes
Percentiles always report lower, more flattering numbers than averages
questions.e: Tail latency is what customers experience when the system is busy.

questions.q: Why is spare capacity (headroom) a design parameter rather than waste?
o: Cloud providers charge less for machines that stay partly idle all month
Idle servers make the system more secure
Latency climbs sharply as utilization nears capacity
Spare capacity is only needed for backups
questions.e: Near full utilization, small load increases cause large latency jumps.

questions.q: An API rate-limits each key and drops low-priority analytics events first when the queue is 80% full. These tactics…
questions.e: Demand-side tactics include sampling, admission control, and prioritization, protecting the checkout path.

questions.q: Adding a Redis cache turns a 120 ms join into a 3 ms lookup for most reads. What new trade-off does it introduce?
o: Higher latency for cached reads than for direct database queries
Staleness, controlled by the cache TTL
questions.e: Caching improves performance but introduces data freshness as a new concern.

questions.q: Using Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR), which change improves availability as much as doubling MTBF?
questions.e: Repair time matters as much as failure frequency.

questions.q: A pod receives a liveness probe every 5 seconds and is replaced after three misses. Which tactics are used?
questions.e: Periodic probes detect the fault; a replacement pod recovers service.

questions.q: Roughly how much yearly downtime does 99.9% availability allow?
questions.e: 99.99% allows about 53 minutes; moving between those tiers often means going from one region to two.

questions.q: A repaired replica replays the write-ahead log, then serves shadow traffic before handling real users. Which tactic family is this?
questions.e: Reintroduction includes resynchronization, shadow operation, and rollback.

questions.q: When does a fault become a failure?
o: Only when the whole system crashes
As soon as it is logged
questions.e: Masking a fault fast enough is a valid availability strategy.

questions.q: A stolen API key still fails because mTLS, IP-range checks, and per-key rate limits also apply. This demonstrates…
questions.e: Independent layered controls avoid any single control being a single point of failure.

questions.q: In STRIDE, an instructor denying they changed a grade is which threat?
questions.e: Repudiation is countered by an append-only audit log.

questions.q: Which four groups do security tactics fall into?
o: Authenticate, authorize, audit, archive, and alert administrators
Detect, resist, react to, and recover from attacks
questions.e: Tactics are grouped by what they do relative to an attack.

questions.q: What does least privilege mainly limit?
o: The network bandwidth each service uses
The damage one compromised part can do
questions.e: A component with minimal rights can do minimal damage if taken over.

questions.q: Adding a payment provider touches one class implementing PaymentGateway plus one config entry. Which quality does this show?
questions.e: Callers depend on the interface, so the change stays in one place.

questions.q: A billing service takes a Clock dependency so tests can set the date to 29 February. Which testability property does this give?
questions.e: Controllability lets a test put the system into a chosen state; observability lets it see the result.

questions.q: How is modifiability measured?
o: By the cost: modules touched, effort, and time
By how many design patterns are used
By the number of comments in the code
By the average response time of the system under representative load
questions.e: Modifiability is about the cost of change.

questions.q: Which is a modifiability tactic?
questions.e: Modifiability tactics reduce module size, increase cohesion, reduce coupling, and defer binding.

questions.q: A long export shows progress, can be cancelled, and leaves no partial file. Which usability tactic group does this belong to?
questions.e: User-initiative tactics include cancel, undo, pause, and aggregate; this also requires running outside the UI thread.

questions.q: Two hospitals both use HL7 FHIR, but one stores blood pressure as one string and the other as two values. What is missing?
questions.e: Standards help but do not guarantee compatible meaning, so a translation layer is still needed.

questions.q: Which is an interoperability tactic?
o: Hashing passwords before they are stored
Adding CPU cores and memory to the shared integration server
Tailoring the interface between mismatched parties
questions.e: Interoperability tactics include discovering services and orchestrating or tailoring interfaces.

questions.q: Why separate UI from domain logic for usability?
o: So cancel, undo, and feedback don't tangle business rules
So the UI can be written in a different language
Because domain logic cannot run on the client, so it must live elsewhere
To remove the need for automated UI testing
questions.e: Separation lets the UI provide feedback and recovery while domain logic stays independent.

questions.q: Write a six-part performance scenario for a search feature.
questions.m: Source: 5,000 concurrent users. Stimulus: submit searches. Environment: exam-week peak. Artifact: catalog search. Response: results returned. Measure: p95 under 500 ms, none over 2 s.

questions.q: Explain binding time with an example and its trade-off.
questions.m: A value can bind at compile time (fast, needs a release), at startup via config, or at run time via a rules table (changed without deploying). Later binding adds flexibility and new failure modes.

questions.q: Using the availability formula, explain why reducing repair time matters.
questions.m: Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). Halving MTTR improves availability as much as doubling MTBF, so fast recovery is as valuable as fewer failures.

questions.q: What is defense in depth? Give an example.
questions.m: Several independent controls so no single one is a point of failure; for example a stolen API key still fails mTLS, IP-range, and rate-limit checks.

questions.q: Explain controllability and observability in testability.
questions.m: Controllability is putting the system into a chosen state (an injected Clock sets the date); observability is seeing the resulting behavior and output.

questions.q: Why don't shared standards guarantee interoperability?
questions.m: Standards align syntax, but systems can still disagree on meaning, such as blood pressure as one string versus two values, so translation is still needed.

questions.q: What distinguishes a documented pattern from a simple template?
o: It states the consequences of applying it
It always includes working source code
It is approved by an industry standards body
It is drawn in standard UML notation
questions.e: A pattern is a problem in context with a solution and consequences; the consequences make it a design tool.

questions.q: Who introduced the pattern form that software engineering adopted in the 1990s?
questions.e: Alexander described building patterns; Gamma and colleagues carried the form into software in 1994.

questions.q: Repository and blackboard belong to which style family?
questions.e: Pipes and filters is data-flow; layered is hierarchical; MVC is interactive; client-server and broker are distributed.

questions.q: What is an architectural style?
o: A feature provided by a specific programming language
Element and connector types plus rules for combining them
A company's coding guidelines and naming rules
A single diagram describing one particular system
questions.e: The constraints are what deliver the style's benefits.

questions.q: A system draws layers but lets any layer call any other. What does it lose?
o: The benefits, since the layering rule isn't enforced
Nothing, since the diagram is what delivers the style's benefits anyway
Only the accuracy of its documentation
Its ability to connect to a database
questions.e: The layered style's value comes from the rule that a layer only calls the layer below.

questions.q: In a closed layered architecture, a layer may call…
o: Any layer above or below it, as long as the call is documented
Only the layer directly below it
questions.e: Open layers permit skipping; closed layers restrict calls to adjacent layers.

questions.q: A read-only lookup passes through a controller, a forwarding service, and a forwarding repository. What anti-pattern is this?
questions.e: Most requests pass through layers that add no logic; opening a layer for pure lookups avoids useless hops.

questions.q: Which is a known cost of layered architecture?
o: It removes separation of concerns between presentation and business logic
The UI can no longer be changed
It cannot run on a single server
questions.e: Benefits include portability and replaceability; costs include latency, duplicate transformations, and pressure to bypass layers.

questions.q: In MVC, what happens after the controller updates the model?
o: The model notifies observing views of the change
The view writes to the database
The controller redraws every view directly with the new values
The model queries each view for its state
questions.e: The model publishes change notifications without knowing specific views (Observer).

questions.q: A spreadsheet's grid, bar chart, and pie chart all update when one cell changes. Which MVC property is shown?
o: Views that update each other directly
A controller that stores the data
questions.e: Views observe the same model and do not know about each other.

questions.q: A CheckoutController computes tax, applies loyalty rules, and calls the payment gateway. What is the problem?
o: Tax logic should live in the view instead
Nothing; this is correct MVC design
It's a fat controller holding model logic
Controllers should never call other code
questions.e: Poor responsibility allocation creates fat controllers and anemic models.

questions.q: Which pattern works inside MVC to keep the model unaware of specific views?
questions.e: The model publishes changes and observers react.

questions.q: What motivated variants such as MVP and MVVM?
o: Removing the model from the pattern
Making presentation logic easier to test
questions.e: They shift presentation logic into a testable presenter or view-model.

questions.q: What limits the throughput of a pipes-and-filters pipeline?
o: The length of the input file name
questions.e: Data can only flow as fast as the bottleneck filter processes it.

questions.q: Which property keeps filters recombinable?
o: Shared global state that every filter in the pipeline can read and update
Each filter calling the next directly
A central controller choosing the order at runtime
A shared data format and no knowledge of neighbouring filters
questions.e: Independent, stateless filters with one format can be reordered and reused.

questions.q: Which workload fits pipes and filters poorly?
o: Filtering a log file with grep, cut, and sort
A CI pipeline of lint, build, and test stages
A compiler's lexer, parser, and optimizer chain
A wizard where users go back to edit earlier steps
questions.e: The style assumes a one-way stream; interactive back-and-forth breaks it.

questions.q: Which concern must a pipes-and-filters design define explicitly?
o: Which filter owns the shared global state
How each filter calls the next one directly
The order in which views are notified
questions.e: Data formats, error propagation, backpressure, and termination all need defining.

questions.q: What does a broker do?
o: Stores all shared data centrally for clients
Compiles client code into server stubs
Renders the views that clients display
Locates servers for clients and forwards requests
questions.e: A broker provides location transparency and loose coupling.

questions.q: A mobile client calls api.shop.com/orders and a gateway picks one of twelve instances. Which pattern provides this?
questions.e: A service registry plus API gateway hides server location from the client.

questions.q: Why is order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity() dangerous across a network?
o: Getters are not allowed in distributed systems
Each call is a network round-trip that can fail
Chained calls cannot be serialized to JSON
questions.e: Remote calls add latency and partial failure; assuming they behave like local calls is a known fallacy.

questions.q: Why should operations that might be retried be idempotent?
o: So it no longer needs authentication
So a retry doesn't repeat the effect, like a double charge
So the operation runs faster on each attempt
So it can keep running normally while the network connection is offline
questions.e: Idempotency makes retries safe under partial failure.

questions.q: In the repository style, what drives control flow?
o: The clients; the shared data is passive
Changes to the data trigger agents
questions.e: In a blackboard, changes to the data drive which agent runs next.

questions.q: Which problem suits a blackboard architecture?
o: Speech recognition, with no fixed solution order
Serving static pages for a website
Payroll calculation with fixed tax rules applied in a set order
questions.e: Specialist agents contribute partial solutions while a controller picks the next contributor.

questions.q: What is a known risk of the repository style?
o: Clients cannot read the shared data
The shared store becomes a bottleneck
questions.e: An IDE where all tools stall when the shared model locks illustrates this.

questions.q: OrderPlaced is consumed by inventory, email, and analytics. What must change to add a loyalty-points consumer?
o: Nothing; the new consumer just subscribes
The order service must call the new consumer
The OrderPlaced schema must be replaced
Every existing consumer must be updated
questions.e: Event-driven fan-out decouples producers from consumers.

questions.q: With at-least-once delivery, how should the email consumer avoid sending two receipts?
o: Key sent mail on the event ID so a duplicate is a no-op
Delete the event queue after each send
Send emails synchronously from the producer so no event is ever needed
questions.e: Consumers must be idempotent because duplicate delivery is expected.

questions.q: What replaces the call stack when debugging an event-driven system?
o: A single log file per server, read in time order across all machines
questions.e: No single stack shows the whole transaction, so tracing links the steps.

questions.q: Which event-driven topology uses an orchestrator for multi-step workflows?
questions.e: The broker topology chains consumers directly for simpler flows.

questions.q: What is the sinkhole anti-pattern and how can it be reduced?
questions.m: Most requests pass through layers that add no logic, paying the cost without benefit. Marking a layer open for pure lookups lets those requests skip useless hops.

questions.q: Explain how MVC keeps views in sync with the model.
questions.m: The controller interprets input and updates the model; the model notifies observing views, which redraw. The model never knows specific views.

questions.q: Give two strengths and one weakness of pipes and filters.
questions.m: Filters can be reused, reordered, and run concurrently. It fits interactive or shared-state workflows poorly, and throughput is limited by the slowest filter.

questions.q: Contrast the repository and blackboard styles.
questions.m: In a repository, data is passive and clients drive control. In a blackboard, specialist agents contribute partial solutions and data changes plus a controller decide who acts next.

questions.q: Why must event consumers be idempotent?
questions.m: At-least-once delivery means events can arrive twice; idempotent handling (for example keyed on the event ID) makes duplicates harmless.

questions.q: Where does detailed design sit in the lifecycle?
o: Before requirements elicitation, as the first lifecycle phase
questions.e: It refines architectural components into implementable structures and behavior.

questions.q: A component quietly opens its own database connection, bypassing the data-access layer. Why is this a detailed-design failure?
o: It ignores architectural decisions from below
Database connections belong in the view layer
Nothing, since faster code is always acceptable
It violates the Liskov substitution principle
questions.e: Detailed design must respect architectural decisions.

questions.q: “enrollment.status — enumeration {PENDING, CONFIRMED, WAITLISTED, DROPPED}; never null.” Which artifact is this?
questions.e: Data dictionaries define each data element's type, values, and rules.

questions.q: A team generates class and sequence diagrams from an undocumented legacy module before changing it. This is…
questions.e: Reverse engineering recovers design knowledge from existing code.

questions.q: How specific should detailed-design output be?
o: Enough that developers don't re-decide structure
As vague as possible to leave room for coders
Exactly the final source code, line by line
Just a list of the class names involved
questions.e: It settles structure so construction does not re-decide it.

questions.q: Generalization and realization model, respectively…
questions.e: Generalization is inheritance; realization connects a classifier to an interface it implements.

questions.q: An Invoice owns InvoiceLines that are deleted with it; a Department references Professors who remain after it is deleted. These are…
questions.e: Composition means the part dies with the whole; aggregation parts outlive it.

questions.q: A report sums shapes.map(Shape::area) with no type checks. Which mechanism makes this work?
questions.e: Each concrete shape supplies its own area(), chosen at run time.

questions.q: Which can be instantiated directly?
questions.e: Abstract classes and methods defer some implementation to subclasses.

questions.q: What is Parnas's criterion for modularization?
o: Split code into modules by execution order
Hide each likely-to-change decision in a module
Give each developer their own module
questions.e: Information hiding localizes likely change.

questions.q: cart.getItems() returns the internal List, so callers can clear it and bypass total recalculation. What is the fix?
o: Add a comment asking callers not to modify the returned list directly
Return an unmodifiable copy so the invariant is preserved
questions.e: Returning internal mutable state breaks encapsulation as surely as a public field.

questions.q: Session storage in Redis is hidden behind a SessionStore interface. What does this buy?
o: A storage change touches one class, not forty
Session code no longer needs any tests
Session data becomes encrypted automatically at rest and in transit
questions.e: Hiding a volatile decision behind an abstraction localizes future change.

questions.q: Encapsulation protects more than private fields. What else does it include?
questions.e: An object must keep its rules true, not only hide its data.

questions.q: A Utils class holds date formatting, password hashing, and CSV parsing. Its cohesion is…
questions.e: Coincidental cohesion is the weakest: parts are grouped for no real reason.

questions.q: Which is the strongest (best) form of cohesion?
questions.e: Cohesion runs from coincidental up to functional.

questions.q: generateReport(type, isPdf, includeCharts) lets the caller steer internal branching. This is…
questions.e: Separate PdfReport and CsvReport implementations remove the flags.

questions.q: Which coupling type is weakest and preferred?
questions.e: Coupling runs from content and common through control and stamp down to data.

questions.q: What does the Single Responsibility Principle really mean?
o: A class should expose only one method
Every method should be a single line
A module answers to one actor or change source
Each file should contain exactly one class
questions.e: SRP is about alignment with a change source, not doing one tiny task.

questions.q: Employee has calculatePay() for finance, reportHours() for operations, and save() for the DBA. What does SRP suggest?
o: Split it so each actor's changes have one home
Merge the three into a single method
Add methods so other actors are served too
questions.e: A class serving several actors will eventually break one while serving another.

questions.q: A growing switch over shipping carriers is replaced with a ShippingCarrier interface and one class per carrier. Which principle is applied?
questions.e: A new carrier is a new class, not an edit to tested code.

questions.q: When does OCP become accidental complexity?
o: When there are more than three subclasses
When extension points have no real variation
questions.e: Speculative flexibility costs complexity without payoff.

questions.q: Square extends Rectangle and forces height to equal width. Code setting width 5 and height 4 gets area 16. Which principle is violated?
questions.e: Signatures matched but behavior did not, so the subtype broke client expectations.

questions.q: According to LSP, a subtype may NOT…
o: Override a method with its own implementation
Declare more fields than its parent class
Add new public methods beyond the parent's
questions.e: Subtypes must accept at least what the parent accepts and guarantee at least what it guarantees.

questions.q: A basic printer must stub scan, fax, and staple from a Printer interface. Which principle fixes this?
questions.e: Split into Printer, Scanner, and FaxMachine so clients depend only on what they use.

questions.q: Under dependency inversion, who should own the abstraction?
questions.e: The detail conforms to policy, so compile-time dependencies point toward the domain.

questions.q: Which statement about dependency injection and dependency inversion is correct?
o: They are two names for the same idea
Injection is a mechanism; inversion is a goal
Inversion can only be done with a DI container
Injecting a dependency always inverts it
questions.e: You can inject a concrete class without inverting any dependency.

questions.q: A constructor takes a PaymentGateway, so a test passes a fake that returns DECLINED. What benefit does this show?
o: Fast, isolated tests with no network
questions.e: Injecting collaborators makes behavior controllable in tests.

questions.q: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?
o: Inheritance is deprecated in modern Java versions
It removes the need to define any interfaces
It always executes faster than inherited code because calls are resolved statically
It can change at run time and avoids fragile base classes
questions.e: Inheritance binds subclass to superclass implementation at compile time.

questions.q: A developer refactors a method and changes its output at the same time. Why is this risky?
o: Compilers and CI tools reject commits that mix both kinds of change together
Refactoring must preserve behavior; mixing both invites outages
Tests cannot run while code is being refactored
Refactoring is expected to change behavior anyway
questions.e: Separate structural changes from behavior changes, protected by automated tests.

questions.q: Which refactoring matches the “long parameter list” smell?
questions.e: Smells point at specific refactorings: long method → extract method, large class → extract class, feature envy → move method.

questions.q:
Trace the call. What value is printed?
interface Shape { int area(); } class Square implements Shape { public int area() { return 5 * 5; } } Shape s = new Square(); System.out.println(s.area());
o: The interface method is called and has no result
questions.e: The variable is typed as Shape, but it refers to a Square object. Dynamic dispatch calls Square.area(), which returns 25.

questions.q:
A client relies on width and height being independent. What is wrong with this result, and what is the soundest design fix?
Rectangle r = new Square(); r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); System.out.println(r.area()); // prints 16
o: No issue: 16 is the expected rectangle area
Square breaks the Rectangle contract; use a common Shape abstraction instead of making Square a Rectangle
The code violates SRP because it has two setters
questions.e: A caller expects independent dimensions and area 20. Square changes that behavior, so it is not safely substitutable for Rectangle (LSP). Model both as shapes with their own area behavior.

questions.q: A single class changes whenever Finance changes pay rules, Operations changes hour reports, or a DBA changes persistence. Which refactoring best applies SRP?
o: Split pay calculation, hour reporting, and persistence into cohesive classes aligned with those change sources
Move every method into a separate one-method class
questions.e: SRP asks for one reason or actor to drive a module’s change. Keep related behavior together while separating the three independent change sources.

questions.q:
The next version must support a new shipping carrier without editing tested checkout logic. Which design is the best OCP fit?
if (carrier.equals("FAST")) ... else if (carrier.equals("POST")) ...
o: Add another else-if for every carrier
Create a CarrierRate interface, implement it per carrier, and have checkout call the interface
Put every carrier’s rules in a global utility class
Use inheritance but keep the same growing type switch
questions.e: A stable abstraction lets a new carrier be added as a new implementation while checkout remains closed to modification.

questions.q: OrderService directly creates MySqlOrderRepository inside its constructor. Which change most directly applies DIP?
o: Have OrderService depend on an OrderRepository abstraction and receive an implementation from outside
Add a second concrete repository field
questions.e: High-level order policy should depend on an abstraction it owns; the database adapter implements that abstraction and can be injected for tests or production.

questions.q:
A BasicPrinter implements this interface but throws UnsupportedOperationException from scan(). What is the best fix?
interface Machine { void print(); void scan(); }
o: Keep the exception; every machine must implement every method
Split the interface into capabilities such as Printable and Scannable, and implement only the needed one
questions.e: ISP keeps interfaces focused. A basic printer should not be forced to promise scanning behavior that it cannot provide.

questions.q:
What is printed by this loop?
Shape[] shapes = { new Circle(2), new Rectangle(3, 4) }; int total = 0; for (Shape shape : shapes) { total += shape.area(); } System.out.println(total);
Assume Circle.area() returns 3 × radius × radius.
o: The loop cannot call area() through Shape
questions.e: Circle.area() is 12 and Rectangle.area() is 12. Each call dispatches to the object’s implementation, so the total is 24.

questions.q:
This getter lets callers clear the order’s internal items and bypass total recalculation. Which fix protects the object’s invariant?
List<Item> getItems() { return items; }
o: Return the internal list and document that callers should not change it
Return an unmodifiable copy or read-only view, and mutate items only through invariant-preserving methods
Recalculate the total only when the object is constructed
questions.e: Encapsulation protects rules as well as fields. A defensive unmodifiable copy prevents external mutation from silently breaking the order total.

questions.q: A NotificationService uses new EmailSender() directly. Later, tests need a fake sender and production may use SMS. What change makes this easier while following the design principles?
o: Add an if statement for test mode
Define a MessageSender abstraction, depend on it, and inject EmailSender, SmsSender, or a fake
Make EmailSender a superclass of NotificationService
Copy NotificationService into a test-only class
questions.e: Depending on an abstraction (DIP) and injecting the collaborator makes the implementation replaceable and the service testable.

questions.q:
The base method accepts any non-negative amount, but an override rejects zero. Which LSP rule does that violate?
// Base contract: amount >= 0 is allowed void transfer(int amount) { ... } // Subtype override rejects amount == 0
o: The base class has too many methods
The subtype added a harmless overload
questions.e: The subtype accepts fewer inputs than the base contract promises. LSP says an override must not strengthen preconditions.

questions.q: A class formats invoices, validates passwords, and parses CSV files. Which response best improves cohesion without over-splitting unrelated tiny methods?
o: Keep the class because each method is useful
Group related behaviors into focused invoice, authentication, and CSV components
Put all three methods in an interface
Move all methods into the application’s main class
questions.e: These responsibilities serve different purposes and change for different reasons. Focused components give each area stronger functional cohesion.

questions.q:
Which design lets a developer add a new payment type with the smallest change to stable code?
double pay(String type, double amount) { if (type.equals("CARD")) ... if (type.equals("WALLET")) ... // new types require another branch }
o: Define a PaymentMethod contract and add a class for each payment method
Put the conditions in a static utility
Use a boolean flag to select the payment type
questions.e: A PaymentMethod abstraction moves variation into implementations; adding a payment method no longer requires changing the stable checkout algorithm (OCP).

questions.q: Distinguish aggregation from composition with an example.
questions.m: Composition: the part dies with the whole (Invoice and InvoiceLine). Aggregation: the part outlives it (Department and Professor).

questions.q: Explain Parnas's information hiding criterion with an example.
questions.m: Modularize around the decisions most likely to change and hide each in a module; for example Redis session storage behind a SessionStore interface.

questions.q: Name the strongest cohesion and weakest coupling and explain why they are preferred.
questions.m: Functional cohesion (one well-defined purpose) and data coupling (only needed data passed) keep changes local and modules understandable.

questions.q: Explain the Liskov Substitution Principle using the Square/Rectangle example.
questions.m: Subtypes must keep client expectations. A Square that forces height = width returns area 16 when the client set 5×4 and expected 20, so it cannot substitute for Rectangle.

questions.q: What is the difference between dependency injection and dependency inversion?
questions.m: Injection supplies collaborators from outside (a mechanism). Inversion makes high-level policy own the abstraction that details implement (a design goal). You can inject without inverting.

questions.q: Why prefer composition over inheritance?
questions.m: Composition can be reconfigured at run time and avoids the fragile base class problem; inheritance binds to the superclass implementation at compile time.

questions.q: What do creational patterns separate clients from?
o: The database schema that stores their objects
questions.e: Clients ask for objects without hard-coding which concrete class is built.

questions.q: Which is the only class-scoped creational pattern?
questions.e: Factory Method varies the product through subclassing; the other four creational patterns are object-scoped.

questions.q: Class-scoped and object-scoped patterns rely mainly on, respectively…
questions.e: Class patterns fix relationships at compile time through inheritance; object patterns vary them at run time through composition.

questions.q: Which part of a pattern entry most directly decides whether you should use it?
questions.e: Consequences state the trade-offs, such as a Singleton's global state and testing cost.

questions.q: Which three purposes classify design patterns?
o: Class, object, and module-level design patterns
questions.e: Scope (class or object) is the second, separate classification axis.

questions.q: In Factory Method, what does the creator class keep, and what does it delegate?
o: Keeps nothing itself; delegates all of the work to a global singleton
Keeps the product-using logic; subclasses pick the product
Keeps the product's fields; delegates its methods
Keeps the concrete classes; delegates the interface
questions.e: Application.openDocument() is written once; createDocument() is overridden.

questions.q: DrawingApplication.createDocument() returns a DrawingDocument and TextApplication returns a TextDocument. Which pattern is this?
questions.e: Subclasses decide which product the shared framework logic receives.

questions.q: Why is Factory Method behind most framework hook points?
o: Frameworks are not allowed to call constructors on application classes
It guarantees the framework has one instance
The framework calls it; your subclass picks the product
It lets the framework copy existing objects
questions.e: Inversion of control: the framework owns the flow, the subclass supplies the product.

questions.q: What is a cost of Factory Method?
questions.e: Each product variation may need a new creator subclass.

questions.q: What problem is Abstract Factory designed to prevent?
o: Creating more than one instance of a class
questions.e: It enforces compatibility within a product family.

questions.q: With Abstract Factory, which change is expensive?
o: Adding a new product kind, such as Slider
Switching between factories at run time
Adding a new platform family, such as Linux
Adding a new client that uses the factory
questions.e: A new family is one new class; a new product type edits the interface and all implementations.

questions.q: How is an Abstract Factory often implemented?
o: A registry of prototype instances cloned on demand
A chain of decorators around a product
A pipeline of filters that build parts
One object whose methods are Factory Methods
questions.e: Abstract Factory is also frequently a Singleton.

questions.q: What does client code depend on in Abstract Factory?
o: The concrete product classes it needs
The SDK of the platform it runs on
questions.e: The client never names a concrete class, so families can be swapped.

questions.q: A constructor with nine nullable parameters is replaced by .size(30).crust(THIN).topping("cheese").build(). Which pattern is this?
questions.e: Builder avoids telescoping constructors for objects with many optional parts.

questions.q: Where does validation belong in a Builder?
o: In build(), once the object is complete
In each setter, as each value arrives from the client
questions.e: build() can reject a pizza with no size.

questions.q: One HouseDirector sequence drives a HouseBuilder and a HouseBlueprintBuilder to produce a house and a printable plan. What does this show?
o: Builders must be implemented as singletons
Blueprints act as prototypes that get cloned
One process can build different representations
questions.e: The director fixes the steps; each concrete builder decides what each step produces.

questions.q: What is Builder's main cost?
questions.e: It trades constructor simplicity for readability and control.

questions.q: When is Prototype a good choice?
o: When related products must come in consistent families
When setup is costly or the type is known only at run time
When exactly one instance must exist in the whole system
When the object has many optional construction parameters
questions.e: Cloning a configured instance skips costly setup.

questions.q: A shallow clone of an Order shares its List<OrderLine>. What happens when the copy's lines are edited?
questions.e: Deep versus shallow copying must be decided deliberately.

questions.q: A diagram editor's toolbar clones a styled rectangle on each drop. What supports this lookup by key?
questions.e: Clients ask the registry for a copy without knowing any concrete class.

questions.q: Why is a naive lazy getInstance() unsafe?
o: It always returns null on the first call
It deep-copies the instance on each call
Two threads can each see null and create one
It cannot be called from static methods
questions.e: An eager static final field, double-checked locking, or an enum fixes it.

questions.q: Which is a reliable way to make a Java Singleton thread-safe?
o: Use an enum or an eager static final field
Clone the instance separately for each calling thread
questions.e: The JVM guarantees uniqueness during class initialization.

questions.q: Tests sharing a singleton cache pass alone but fail together. Why?
o: State leaks between tests through the global instance
Singletons cannot be tested at all
The test framework creates a new singleton for every test class it loads
questions.e: Injecting a single instance through a container gives single lifetime without global state.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say singletons hide dependencies?
o: Singletons are loaded by a separate class loader
Singletons are always declared as private classes
Callers use it without declaring it as a dependency
questions.e: Hidden dependencies make code harder to test and reason about.

questions.q: When should Singleton be used?
o: Whenever an object is used in many places
For every service class in the application
Only when one instance is a real invariant
To avoid passing parameters between classes
questions.e: Dependency injection often gives single-instance lifetime more cleanly.

questions.q: Families of widgets that must stay consistent across a platform suggest which pattern?
questions.e: Many kinds of one product → Factory Method; one product with many parts → Builder; costly setup → Prototype.

questions.q: What is the recommended starting point before adding a creational pattern?
o: An Abstract Factory from the first version
A Builder for every object, however simple
A Singleton for every class that is created, to keep instances under control
A plain constructor until construction starts varying
questions.e: Prefer the simplest mechanism that keeps the needed flexibility.

questions.q: Factories, Builder, and Prototype each primarily vary…
o: Compile time, link time, and run time binding
The view, controller, and model of creation
What type, how it is assembled, and copying state
Speed, memory use, and security of creation
questions.e: Choose by what varies: what, how, or when objects are created.

questions.q: Compare Factory Method and Abstract Factory by scope and what they vary.
questions.m: Factory Method is class-scoped and varies the product through subclassing. Abstract Factory is object-scoped and swaps a factory object to produce a consistent family of products.

questions.q: What is the rigidity cost of Abstract Factory?
questions.m: Adding a new family is one class, but adding a new product kind (such as Slider) changes the abstract factory interface and every implementation.

questions.q: Why does Builder put validation in build()?
questions.m: Only at build() is the object known to be complete, so it can reject invalid combinations such as a pizza with no size.

questions.q: Explain the shallow vs deep copy hazard in Prototype.
questions.m: A shallow clone shares references, so editing the copy's list edits the original. A deep clone copies the referenced objects too.

questions.q: Give two drawbacks of Singleton and one alternative.
questions.m: It creates global state that leaks between tests and hides dependencies (and naive lazy init is not thread-safe). Dependency injection can provide a single instance without the global.

questions.q: The app expects PaymentGateway.charge(Money) but the SDK offers StripeClient.createCharge(long cents, String currency). Which pattern fits?
questions.e: Adapter translates one interface into the one the client expects.

questions.q: Object adapters and class adapters use, respectively…
questions.e: Class adapters need multiple inheritance or similar language support.

questions.q: What is the key timing difference between Adapter and Bridge?
o: Both are only applied at run time
Neither is used when writing new code
Adapter is retrofitted; Bridge is designed in up front
Bridge is retrofitted; Adapter is designed in up front
questions.e: Adapter reconciles existing unrelated code; Bridge plans for two independent dimensions.

questions.q: What does an Adapter change?
o: The core responsibility, not the interface
The interface, not the core responsibility
questions.e: The adaptee still does the work; the adapter only translates.

questions.q: What is a two-way adapter?
o: One shared by exactly two client classes
One that also caches the adaptee's results
One that wraps two separate adaptee objects
One implementing both interfaces for either side
questions.e: It lets both old and new code treat the object as their own type.

questions.q: Three shapes and three renderers would need nine subclasses. How many classes does Bridge need?
questions.e: Bridge turns m × n into m + n; adding a fourth renderer adds one class.

questions.q: Before applying Bridge, what must you identify?
o: An expensive object to load lazily
questions.e: Bridge separates an abstraction dimension from an implementation dimension.

questions.q: JDBC code written against Connection and Statement while vendors supply drivers is an example of…
questions.e: The abstraction side (JDBC API) and implementation side (drivers) vary independently.

questions.q: In Bridge, what is a refined abstraction?
o: An extension of the abstraction side only
A proxy that caches implementor calls
A concrete implementor of the bridge
questions.e: Each side can grow on its own.

questions.q: A backup tool calls getSize() on the root folder without checking whether each node is a file or folder. Which pattern enables this?
questions.e: Leaves and composites share one interface; folders sum their children recursively.

questions.q: In the transparent Composite variant, where do child-management methods such as add() live?
o: Only on the leaf class, never the composite
Only on the composite class, never on the leaf, so leaves cannot misuse them
On the component, so add() on a leaf fails at run time
In a separate visitor that walks the tree
questions.e: The safe variant puts them only on the composite, trading uniformity for type safety.

questions.q: What is the main power of Composite?
o: It makes tree traversal much faster
It prevents cycles in the tree automatically
Clients never check leaf versus branch
It removes the need for any recursion
questions.e: Uniform treatment of parts and wholes simplifies client code.

questions.q: Which concerns need care when using Composite?
o: Thread-safe lazy initialization of each leaf
questions.e: Trees can accidentally become graphs or share children.

questions.q: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(f))) is an example of…
questions.e: Buffering and decoding are added by wrapping, not by a BufferedDecodingFileReader subclass.

questions.q: Compress-then-encrypt produces a small file; encrypt-then-compress barely compresses. What does this show about decorators?
o: Only one decorator can be applied
They must be applied in alphabetical order
questions.e: Same wrappers, different order, different results.

questions.q: Why can't a client tell a decorated object from a plain one?
o: It shares the interface and forwards calls
It replaces and deletes the original object
The client never calls the wrapped object
It is a subclass of the client class
questions.e: Transparency is what lets decorators stack.

questions.q: What is a known cost of many small decorators?
o: Loss of the component's original interface
Harder debugging and unclear object identity
questions.e: Deep wrapper stacks can be hard to trace.

questions.q: TripFacade.bookTrip() calls flight, hotel, car, payment, and email subsystems and rolls back on failure. Which pattern is this?
questions.e: Facade gives a simpler entry point to a complex subsystem.

questions.q: Does a Facade forbid direct use of the subsystem?
o: No; advanced users can still call it directly
Yes; every call must pass through the facade
Only when used in a layered architecture
Only for read operations, not writes
questions.e: The facade covers the common cases without locking out the rest.

questions.q: What separates Facade from Adapter and Mediator?
o: It controls access to a single object
It translates one interface into another
It simplifies an interface without adding features
It coordinates peer objects that would otherwise talk to each other directly
questions.e: Adapter translates; Mediator coordinates colleagues; Facade simplifies.

questions.q: What risk does the chapter warn about for Facade?
o: Growing into an all-knowing god object
questions.e: A facade should stay a thin entry point.

questions.q: A document shows placeholders and loads each 8 MP image only when it scrolls into view. Which proxy type is this?
questions.e: Virtual proxies defer expensive creation until needed.

questions.q: AdminServiceProxy checks the caller's role before forwarding. Which proxy type is this?
questions.e: Authorization lives in one wrapper instead of at the top of every method.

questions.q: Proxy and Decorator share a structure. What distinguishes them?
o: A proxy must always be remote
Proxy changes the interface; Decorator does not
Decorator is only used for I/O streams
Intent: access control versus added behavior
questions.e: Both wrap an object with the same interface; their purpose differs.

questions.q: Why must a remote proxy not hide latency and failure misleadingly?
o: Callers must still handle delays and partial failure
Remote calls through a proxy never fail
Remote proxies are always faster than local calls
questions.e: Preserving the interface should not pretend a remote call is local.

questions.q: Which is a smart-reference proxy responsibility?
o: Summing the sizes of child nodes
Translating a legacy interface into the one clients expect
Reference counting or locking around the subject
Building an object step by step
questions.e: Smart references add bookkeeping around access.

questions.q: Explain how Bridge avoids class explosion with numbers.
questions.m: Without Bridge, m abstractions × n implementations need m×n classes (3 shapes × 3 renderers = 9). With Bridge it is m + n (6), and a new renderer adds one class.

questions.q: Compare the transparent and safe Composite variants.
questions.m: Transparent puts child methods on the component, so leaves must reject add() at run time. Safe puts them only on the composite, gaining type safety but requiring client type checks.

questions.q: Why does decorator order matter? Give an example.
questions.m: Each wrapper transforms what the next sees. Compress-then-encrypt gives a small ciphertext; encrypt-then-compress gives near-random bytes that barely compress.

questions.q: Distinguish Proxy from Decorator.
questions.m: Both wrap an object with the same interface. Proxy controls access (lazy loading, protection, remote); Decorator adds responsibilities.

questions.q: Distinguish Adapter from Facade.
questions.m: Adapter translates one interface into another that a client expects. Facade provides a simpler interface to a complex subsystem without changing what it can do.

questions.q: What is the main goal of architecture evaluation?
o: A pass/fail grade for the architect and the design team
Informed decisions about risks and trade-offs
questions.e: Evaluation is not a beauty contest; it exposes risks, sensitivity points, and trade-offs.

questions.q: When is the cheapest time to fix an architectural mistake?
o: After the first production incident shows the real weakness
While the architecture is still a document
questions.e: A shared database found in review is a design change; after launch it is a migration and a maintenance window.

questions.q: Which is a common side benefit of the first evaluation session?
o: Documentation is no longer needed once the evaluation has finished
The documented architecture differs from real intent
The project budget is usually increased
questions.e: Evaluation forces clarity and alignment.

questions.q: When should evaluation be repeated?
o: When drivers or the architecture change
Only after production failures reveal a problem
questions.e: Evaluate early and again when the basis for decisions changes.

questions.q: A question is only about how costly three planned changes will be. Which method fits best?
questions.e: SAAM focuses on scenario-based modifiability analysis.

questions.q: A half-designed shared component must be usable by other teams. Which method fits?
questions.e: ARID reviews an intermediate design with its future users.

questions.q: A finished architecture has competing performance and security goals. Which method fits?
questions.e: ATAM analyzes trade-offs among multiple quality attributes.

questions.q: How does ATAM relate to SAAM?
o: ATAM extended SAAM to all qualities and trade-offs
ATAM evaluates code while SAAM evaluates designs
SAAM was created later to replace ATAM
They are two names for the same method
questions.e: SAAM came first; ATAM added trade-off analysis across qualities.

questions.q: In an ARID session, what do reviewers do that surfaces usability gaps quickly?
o: Write pseudocode using the draft interface
Vote on the diagram's notation and colors
Rewrite the component from scratch themselves
questions.e: Active design review makes reviewers use the design, not just read it.

questions.q: The number of web-server replicas strongly affects availability and nothing else. It is a…
questions.e: A sensitivity point affects one quality attribute.

questions.q: Raising message-bus encryption improves confidentiality but worsens latency. This is a…
questions.e: A trade-off point affects multiple qualities and needs an explicit decision.

questions.q: “The failover procedure has never been tested under load” is recorded as a…
questions.e: Risks are potentially problematic decisions or gaps.

questions.q: Why record non-risks?
o: They replace the utility tree in the report
They list decisions that will become risks
They pad the report to a required length
They show which decisions were checked and sound
questions.e: A non-risk shows what was analyzed and why it is acceptable.

questions.q: Which ATAM phase widens participation to the broader stakeholder group?
questions.e: Phase 1 works with the core team; phase 2 involves the broader stakeholders; phase 3 delivers the report and follow-up.

questions.q: Which is an ATAM output?
o: A deployment script for each environment
Risks, non-risks, sensitivity and trade-off points
The production source code, build scripts, and release notes
A signed contract with the vendor
questions.e: Outputs also include analyzed approaches and prioritized scenarios.

questions.q: What does a lightweight ATAM keep?
o: Scenario and trade-off reasoning, less ceremony
Only the final report, without any of the analysis behind it
questions.e: It trims process while retaining the core analysis.

questions.q: What is the structure of a utility tree?
o: Module → class → method → line of code
questions.e: Each leaf is a concrete scenario rated by importance and difficulty.

questions.q: Which utility tree leaves are analyzed first?
questions.e: They carry the most business value and the most architectural uncertainty.

questions.q: In a utility tree rating such as (H, M), what do the two letters represent?
o: Hazard severity and likelihood of attack
Cache hit rate and mean response time
questions.e: Ratings guide which scenarios get detailed analysis.

questions.q: Twelve scenarios are brainstormed but there is time to analyze four. How are they chosen?
o: The architect picks the ones they prefer
The four easiest ones are chosen first
Stakeholders vote; top scenarios are analyzed
They are taken in alphabetical order
questions.e: Prioritization focuses limited evaluation time.

questions.q: A failover is traced: detect 5 s, drain 3 s, promote 10 s, total 18 s against a 30 s target, with promotion untested. What should the report make visible?
o: That the promotion step is an untested assumption
That the requirement is met, so nothing else matters
That the target should be raised
questions.e: Tracing a scenario through structures must show where evidence is weak.

questions.q: A team claims a 90% cache hit rate with no measurement. How should evaluators record it?
o: As an assumption, with a measurement advised
As a non-risk, since caches are standard
As a trade-off point for the cache
questions.e: "We believe" is an assumption; a load test result is evidence.

questions.q: What is a risk theme?
o: Related risks grouped by the driver they threaten
The list of stakeholders who attended
The visual style used in the final report
A single untested component that threatens the system's availability
questions.e: Themes such as "operational readiness is unaddressed" make findings actionable for management.

questions.q: What should each evaluation finding leave the review with?
o: A new architect assigned to the project
An owner and a follow-up date
questions.e: Re-evaluation then checks whether mitigation changed the risk profile.

questions.q: Distinguish a sensitivity point from a trade-off point with examples.
questions.m: A sensitivity point affects one quality (replica count → availability). A trade-off point affects several (encryption level → confidentiality up, latency worse).

questions.q: When would you choose ATAM, SAAM, or ARID?
questions.m: ATAM for finished architectures with competing qualities; SAAM for modifiability questions about planned changes; ARID for reviewing an intermediate design with its future users.

questions.q: Describe a utility tree and how its leaves are prioritized.
questions.m: Utility → quality attribute → refinement → concrete scenario. Each leaf is rated by business importance and architectural difficulty; (H,H) leaves are analyzed first.

questions.q: Why must evaluators separate assumptions from evidence?
