questions.m: "We believe it is fast enough" is an assumption; a load-test result is evidence. Blurring them hides risk, so assumptions are flagged with recommended measurements.

questions.q: What is a risk theme and why is it useful?
questions.m: A risk theme groups related risks and maps them to the business driver they endanger, which makes findings actionable for management.

questions.q: Why is one 90-page document for both new developers and operations a poor choice?
o: Developers only need the source code to work
Long documents cannot be kept in version control alongside the source code
Operations teams do not read design documents
Each audience needs different content, so neither is served
questions.e: Developers need module views and build steps; operations needs deployment, monitoring, and failure modes.

questions.q: The retry policy is written once in a cross-cutting section and referenced from each view. What principle does this apply?
o: A single source of truth, no repetition
Adding a variability guide per view
Giving each view a primary presentation
questions.e: A change cannot then leave three views disagreeing.

questions.q: When is documentation ready to be declared done?
o: When every UML diagram type is included
When it reaches the target page count
Once its intended readers find it fit to use
When the lead architect has signed it
questions.e: Documentation nobody can act on is not documentation.

questions.q: Which set lists the parts of a view document?
o: Risks, owners, dates, priorities, and status
Classes, methods, fields, code comments, and the unit tests for each
Title, author, date, reviewers, and signature
questions.e: Each part answers a different reader question about the view.

questions.q: “NotificationService provides send(Notification), requires TemplateStore, may not be called synchronously from checkout.” This belongs in the…
questions.e: The catalog defines responsibilities, interfaces, and relationships of each element.

questions.q: “Identity provider is a build-time choice among LDAP, Azure AD, or Okta.” This belongs in the…
questions.e: Variability guides record permitted options and when they are bound.

questions.q: What does a view's context section show?
o: Every class in the system in detail
The view's boundary and external dependencies
The team's schedule, availability, and on-call rotation for the view
The history of the project so far
questions.e: Context places the view within its surroundings.

questions.q: Which approach separates conceptual, module, execution, and code views?
questions.e: 4+1 uses logical, process, development, physical, and scenarios.

questions.q: The C4 model nests which levels?
questions.e: C4 is a widely used modern variant, often a fast fit for microservices teams.

questions.q: A table maps the billing module to the billing-api container on two nodes. Why does this matter?
o: It keeps module and deployment views consistent
It is required only when using RUP
It replaces the need for a deployment view
It serves as the project glossary
questions.e: Consistency and mappings prevent contradictory documentation.

questions.q: How should views be chosen?
o: By producing every UML diagram type available
From stakeholder concerns, not every possible model
By copying the set used in another project
By using the modeling tool's default templates
questions.e: Each selected view should answer a real stakeholder question.

questions.q: “All service errors return RFC 7807 problem details and retries use exponential backoff with jitter.” Where does this belong?
questions.e: It belongs to no single view but constrains all of them.

questions.q: “Student” meant applicant, enrolled learner, and debtor to three offices. Which artifact solves this?
questions.e: A glossary prevents one word meaning different things to different teams.

questions.q: What is the role of the documentation roadmap?
o: Telling readers where to look for each question
Showing the network topology of the system
Listing release dates for each version
questions.e: It is the entry point that makes a large package usable.

questions.q: Which documentation element preserves decision context and consequences?
questions.e: ADRs capture context, decision, alternatives, consequences, and status.

questions.q: An arrow from A to B could mean “calls”, “data flows to”, “depends on”, or “sends a message to”. What fixes this?
o: A key that defines each line style
questions.e: Without a key, four readers form four architectures.

questions.q: Instead of one diagram with 60 services, a team ships a 6-box context diagram and six focused container diagrams. What principle is applied?
o: Automated diagrams are always the better choice
A diagram should show everything at once
One diagram per question, at a readable scope
Diagrams should be replaced by prose only
questions.e: A diagram that answers five questions answers none well.

questions.q: What is the limit of automatically generated diagrams?
o: They stay fresh but can't capture intent
They are always inaccurate and misleading
They cannot be stored in version control
questions.e: Generated dependency graphs show facts; why payments must not call reporting is written by hand.

questions.q: Why does documentation outside the definition of done go stale?
o: Reviewers delete old documents each release
Nothing forces it to change when code changes
questions.e: Making documentation part of done keeps it current.

questions.q: Architecture docs and PlantUML sources live in the repo and are reviewed in the same pull request as the code. This is…
questions.e: An undocumented structural change then fails review.

questions.q: Which facts should generated artifacts carry?
o: The glossary definitions of domain terms
The rationale behind key design decisions
The fast-changing ones, like dependency graphs
questions.e: Generated facts stay fresh for free; rationale must be written by people.

questions.q: Which describes useful documentation?
o: Diagrams only, with no written text
Concise to maintain, detailed enough to act on
As long and exhaustive as possible so nothing is ever missed
Written once and then never changed
questions.e: Balance maintainability with actionability.

questions.q: List the parts of a view document and what each provides.
questions.m: Primary presentation (diagram plus key), element catalog (responsibilities and interfaces), context (boundary and external dependencies), variability guide (permitted options), and rationale (why, and rejected alternatives).

questions.q: Why does every diagram need a key? Give an example.
questions.m: Boxes and lines are ambiguous; an arrow could mean calls, data flow, dependency, or messaging. A key fixes one meaning so readers share one architecture.

questions.q: What is a cross-cutting concept? Give an example.
questions.m: A rule that belongs to no single view but constrains all of them, such as all service errors using RFC 7807 and retries using exponential backoff with jitter.

questions.q: Explain how to keep architecture documentation living.
questions.m: Version docs with code, review them in the same pull request, make them part of the definition of done, and generate the fast-changing facts while writing rationale by hand.

questions.q: Compare 4+1, Siemens Four-Views, and C4.
questions.m: 4+1: logical, process, development, physical plus scenarios. Siemens: conceptual, module, execution, code. C4: context, container, component, code.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why software architecture is considered a foundational design activity?
o: It focuses on low-level coding decisions
It establishes the groundwork for satisfying functional and non-functional requirements
questions.e: Correct. Architecture sets the high-level structure that makes it possible to meet both the functional and the non-functional (quality) requirements. Every later design decision builds on it.

questions.q: Why are multiple architectural views required in complex systems?
o: Because no single view can represent all system aspects for all stakeholders
questions.e: Correct. Each stakeholder cares about different concerns. Users care about function, operators about deployment, developers about modules. One diagram cannot answer all of those at once.

questions.q: Which architectural view mainly contributes to evaluating scalability and performance?
questions.e: Correct. The process view covers runtime concerns: processes, concurrency, distribution and communication. Performance and scalability are judged from these.

questions.q: Design synchronicity ensures that:
o: All phases stay aligned with architecture, especially implementation
questions.e: Correct. Design synchronicity means the implementation (and every other phase) stays faithful to the architecture, so design and code don’t drift apart.

questions.q: Software architecture is NOT about:
questions.e: Correct. Algorithms are low-level detail handled in detailed or construction design, not in architecture.

questions.q: Which task is part of architectural design?
questions.e: Correct. Architectural design starts by identifying the stakeholders and their concerns, because those concerns drive the architecture and choose which views are needed.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The requirements activity in which stakeholder needs are discovered using techniques such as interviews and observation is called ___.
questions.e: The correct term is elicitation — the discovery step, before anything is documented.

questions.q: An architect interviews end users, observes their current work, and runs a facilitated workshop to discover system needs. Which requirements activity is being performed?
questions.e: Interviews, observation, and facilitated meetings are common elicitation techniques.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Checking whether documented requirements correctly represent stakeholder needs is called requirements ___.
questions.e: Requirements validation checks that the documented requirements are appropriate and correct.

questions.q: Two stakeholder groups request requirements that cannot both be fully satisfied. Which activity is most directly used to resolve this conflict?
questions.e: Negotiation is used to resolve conflicts and reach acceptable trade-offs among requirements.

questions.q: Match each architecture process activity with its main purpose.
pairs: Define major structures and design decisions
Assess whether the architecture satisfies important concerns
Check that implementation remains consistent with the architecture
questions.e: Architecture is an iterative process extending from understanding requirements through implementation oversight.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: After designing an architecture, the activity used to determine whether it satisfies important requirements and stakeholder concerns is architecture ___.
questions.e: Architecture evaluation checks whether architectural decisions adequately address requirements and concerns.

questions.q: A student rejects a valid design because she assumes a component can only be used in the same way she has seen it used before. Which concept best explains this limitation?
questions.e: Functional fixedness restricts problem solving by tying thinking to familiar uses or assumptions.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Breaking a complex software system into smaller, manageable parts is called ___.
questions.e: The correct term is modularization.

questions.q: Abstraction helps designers manage complexity by focusing on essential characteristics and hiding unnecessary details.
questions.e: Abstraction deliberately suppresses lower-level detail so the designer can reason at the appropriate level.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: When two designs satisfy the same requirements, the design with fewer unnecessary dependencies is generally preferred because software design should minimize ___.
questions.e: A key design consideration is minimizing unnecessary complexity.

questions.q: Match each design concept with the description that best represents it.
pairs: Rely on familiar uses or unstated assumptions that restrict solutions
Focus on essential characteristics while hiding unnecessary details
Divide a system into smaller manageable parts
Generate and compare possible solutions after understanding the problem
questions.e: These concepts describe core approaches and limitations in software design problem solving.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The high-level organization of a software system, including its major elements and relationships, is its software ___.
questions.e: The correct term is architecture.

questions.q: A team is deciding the major components of a system, how they interact, and how the design will support performance and security. At what level are they primarily working?
questions.e: Software architecture addresses high-level system structures, interactions, and quality concerns.

questions.q: Software architecture is concerned only with functional structure and does not need to consider non-functional requirements.
questions.e: Architecture must address both system structure and important quality attributes such as performance, security, and availability.

questions.q: The requirement "The system should respond quickly" is sufficiently specific and verifiable for architectural evaluation.
questions.e: Terms such as "usually" and "quickly" are vague unless replaced by measurable criteria.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A design decision intended to influence or control the response associated with a quality attribute is called an architectural ___.
questions.e: The correct term is tactic — one decision aimed at one quality-attribute response.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The 4+1 view that emphasizes the major functional elements of the system and their relationships is the ___ view.
questions.e: The logical view represents the main functional abstractions and relationships.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The 4+1 view that focuses on the organization of source-code modules, packages, and development units is the ___ view.
questions.e: The development view describes the static organization of software in the development environment.

questions.q: Which 4+1 view should an architect emphasize when analyzing concurrent execution, communication among running processes, and synchronization?
questions.e: The process view captures runtime behavior, processes or threads, communication, and synchronization.

questions.q: A deployment engineer wants to know which software elements run on which servers and hardware nodes. Which 4+1 view is most useful?
questions.e: The physical view shows deployment and mapping of software onto hardware.

questions.q: Match each 4+1 architectural view with its primary concern.
pairs: Major functional elements and their relationships
Organization of software modules and packages
Deployment of software onto hardware nodes
Use cases that illustrate and validate the architecture
questions.e: The 4+1 model uses multiple complementary views to address different architectural concerns.

questions.q: Match each quality attribute scenario element with its meaning.
pairs: Event or condition that affects the system
System element affected by the stimulus
Condition under which the stimulus occurs
What the system does after the stimulus
Measurable criterion used to evaluate the response
questions.e: A complete quality attribute scenario contains source, stimulus, artifact, environment, response, and response measure.

questions.q: Match each quality attribute scenario element with the correct part of the scenario.
pairs: Attempts to submit an assignment for the first time
Provides instructions, guides file upload, and confirms successful submission
Within 2 minutes, without external help, no more than one input error
questions.e: This scenario focuses on usability: ease of learning, ease of use, and task-completion time.

questions.q: Which FOUR of the following are key tasks performed during the Software Architecture Design effort?
o: Installing the software on end-user devices
Identifying the system’s major components and interfaces
Writing the source code for system components
Identifying stakeholders’ concerns and quality attributes
Creating the project budget and staff schedule
questions.e: Software architecture design focuses on stakeholders and quality attributes, architectural views, architectural styles/patterns, and the system’s major components and interfaces. Algorithm design, coding, testing, deployment, maintenance, training, budgeting, and debugging belong to other activities.

questions.q: Which FOUR of the following are considered major Software Design Challenges?
questions.e: The four major design challenges tested here are requirements volatility, inconsistent development processes, fast and ever-changing technology, and managing design influences.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following are the main major activities in the Software Design Process?
questions.e: The two major activities are Software Architecture and Detailed Design.

questions.q: A student rejects a valid design because she assumes a component can only be used in the same way she has seen it used before. Which concept best explains this limitation?
questions.e: Functional fixedness restricts problem solving by tying thinking to familiar uses or assumptions.

questions.q: Heartbeat is a performance tactic used to reduce response time.
questions.e: Heartbeat is an availability tactic used for fault detection. It monitors whether a component is still functioning; it is not a performance tactic for reducing response time.

questions.q: The '+1' view represents the database structure of the system.
questions.e: False. In Kruchten’s 4+1 model, the '+1' represents scenarios or use cases that illustrate and validate the other architectural views; it is not the database structure.

questions.q: According to the IEEE definition, which of the following best describes Software Engineering?
o: The artistic creation of computer programs and hardware.
The application of a systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable approach to the development, operation, and maintenance of software.
A methodical procedure for writing code in a specific programming language.
A process focused solely on finding and fixing bugs after delivery.
questions.e: IEEE defines software engineering as the application of a systematic, disciplined, quantifiable approach to the development, operation and maintenance of software.

questions.q: In the context of engineering problem-solving, what is "functional fixedness"?
o: A state where a solution is successfully validated and the goal is reached.
A design strategy that focuses strictly on functional requirements.
A cognitive bias that limits the ability to find solutions because objects are only seen in their usual function.
The process of fixing errors in the final implementation phase.
questions.e: Functional fixedness is a mental block: you only see an object or component in its usual role, which limits the solutions you consider.

questions.q: Which phase of the holistic problem-solving framework is performed during the "Initial State"?
o: Interpreting the problem and evaluating constraints.
questions.e: In the initial state you interpret the problem and evaluate constraints (cost, schedule, quality). Brainstorming and synthesis come in the intermediate states.

questions.q: From a project management perspective, why is studying software design important?
o: It ensures that only one person owns the entire system.
It helps minimize the negative effects of requirements volatility.
It focuses purely on technical artifacts like class diagrams.
It eliminates the need for testing and maintenance phases.
questions.e: Good design lets the project absorb changing requirements with less damage, which is why managers care about it.

questions.q: Which software design challenge refers to the growth or change in requirements during a project’s development lifecycle?
questions.e: Requirements volatility is the growth or change of requirements during development.

questions.q: Which design activity corresponds to a "macro-design approach" that provides black-box models to evaluate system quality?
questions.e: Software architecture is the macro-design approach: black-box models of the major components used to reason about system quality.

questions.q: What is the primary focus of "Detailed Design"?
o: External properties of software components and non-functional requirements.
The overall development process for both hardware and software.
The internals of system components and their behavior to fulfill functional requirements.
Project management tasks like staffing and tracking.
questions.e: Detailed design opens the black boxes: the internals of each component and how they behave to meet the functional requirements.

questions.q: The principle of "Abstraction" is best described as:
o: Decomposing a system into fine-grained components.
Focusing on essential characteristics of entities while deferring unnecessary details.
Exposing all internal data to ensure other modules can access it easily.
Combining hardware and software into a single monolithic unit.
questions.e: Abstraction keeps the essential characteristics in view and defers the details. Decomposition into components is modularization.

questions.q: In software design principles, "Coupling" refers to:
o: The degree of interdependence between software modules.
How well tasks within a single module relate to one another.
Ensuring a module provides all required services.
Hiding the implementation details of a class.
questions.e: Coupling is the interdependence between modules. Option b describes cohesion, c completeness, d encapsulation.

questions.q: Which design principle measures how well a unit provides only the services necessary for its intent, ensuring no extra, unnecessary features are included?
questions.e: Sufficiency: the unit provides only the services it needs for its intent. Completeness is the opposite check: it provides all the services it should.
